messages.subject: Vectorizing over 2-dimensional structures in "deep interactions" model?
parts:
Vectorizing over 2-dimensional structures in "deep interactions" model?

------------------------------------------------------------

Hey guys,

I'm running a "deep interactions" model, i.e. similar to what Andy and I just published in AJPS -- code below.  This time I'm (a) using Stan via rstan, and (b) fitting a much bigger model with more groups and more interactions.  I am successfully fitting the model, but it's taking a *very* long time, on the order of ~4 days to fit.  I'm wondering if I can do some extra vectorization to speed it up.  Code is attached.  Any suggestions?

Some specifics that I can point out:

I'm fitting a logit with ~30,000 cases after missing value imputation.  There are 16 continuous variables, all rescaled to mean = 0, sd = 0.5 (the z_ variables).  There are 9 sets of group-level variables, all 9 of which are interacted with each other, in the form of varying intercepts.  Most of the groups have < 5 levels, with a couple of exceptions.  In particular:

n_sex = 2
n_eth = 4
n_inc = 5
n_mar = 2
n_edu = 2
n_age = 4
n_pid = 3
n_prmd = 7
n_votes = 3

But the model gets big when I do all the two-way interactions between all of these.

I think the big computational slow-down comes in all the looping, but it's unclear to me how to avoid it.  There are two types of loops: (1) The "deep interactions" are all two-dimensional structures, so I think I have to go through these loops to set the normalization priors; (2) I think I have to set the varying intercepts (assigning alpha_groups) through this loop.  Is there any way to vectorize either of these steps?

I ran this once, 8 chains at 2500 iterations, parallelized over 8 cores.  Some of the chains finished relatively quickly, but the last chain finished about 4 days later.  Each core here is 2.00 GHz on a linux box where memory is not a problem, so I shouldn't be paging out.

Any tips on how to make this faster?  One thing I can do is upgrade stan -- I'm currently on rstan 1.1.0 -- but I think the real gains are through vectorization, or anything else you might suggest.  Any help is appreciated ... thanks!

Last thing, I saw that you ask for the sessionInfo() from R.  I'm pasting it here, from the moment before I run the full model.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Vectorizing over 2-dimensional structures in "deep interactions" model?
parts:
Yair -- I think you missed the attachment.
The mailing list can't handle .stan suffixes,
but if you append .txt, they'll go through.

By all means you should definitely upgrade to
the latest Stan. We're making it much faster
as we go, and it's only the later releases that have
vectorized all the distributions.

Loops per se aren't a problem -- they're compiled.
But vectorizing probability functions can really help
because we optimize the gradient calcs at the same time
and it really cuts down on non-branch-predictable
virtual function calls. So it helps to run a loop to
construct a vector to pass into a probability function.
The loop itself will hardly take any time at all if it
just does simple arithmetic or index fiddling.

> I ran this once, 8 chains at 2500 iterations, parallelized over 8 cores. Some of the chains finished relatively
> quickly, but the last chain finished about 4 days later.

It also sounds like your model's a good candidate
for what Andrew's been asking for -- something that
will run by time rather than number of chains. We
don't trust the chains that start in the weeds anyway.

On that note, one thing you can do is try init=0, which
is a much better starting point for regressions (unbounded
params init to 0, positive bounded params to 1, bounded
both way params init to the middle of their range).

I've been meaning to figure out what, if any, overhead
is added by RStan over the command line. Jiqiang has things
sorted out now so you can dump data through RStan in a readable
to command-line-Stan format, then run the command-line Stan itself,
which streams output, and then read it back into R for analysis
with Stan (and anything else you want in R).

One of the things we saw slowing down this kind of model was
covariance matrix priors with 0.99 off-diagonal correlations.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Vectorizing over 2-dimensional structures in "deep interactions" model?
parts:
A couple things that will speed things up a bit. First, all the lines like:

for (i in 1:n_sex) {
alpha_sex_eth[i] ~ normal(0, sigma_sex_eth);
....
}

Can just be:

alpha_sex_eth ~ normal(0, sigma_sex_eth);

Also, in general, when you have things that look like a*b + c*d + ...

It is faster to create two temporary vectors v1 = [a, c, ...] and v2 =
[b, d, ...] and replace the expression with dot_product(v1,v2)

Along a similar vein, if you're adding a lot of things up (a + b + c +
d + ...), it can sometimes be faster to create a temporary vector v =
[a, b, c, d, ...] and write sum(v).

Basically, in Stan copying is cheap but operations are expensive so
saving operations either by caching and reusing computations or using
single vector operations in place of multiple scalar operations will
generally make things much faster.

Cheers,
Marcus

P.S. It looks like you add alpha_sex_eth[sex[i_n], eth[i_n]] twice,
I'm guessing this is a bug?

Also, in general, when you have things that look like a*b + c*d + ...

It is faster to create two temporary vectors v1 = [a, c, ...] and v2 =
[b, d, ...] and replace the expression with dot_product(v1,v2)

d + ...), it can sometimes be faster to create a temporary vector v =
[a, b, c, d, ...] and write sum(v).

Basically, in Stan copying is cheap but operations are expensive so
saving operations either by caching and reusing computations or using
single vector operations in place of multiple scalar operations will
generally make things much faster.

Cheers,

parts:
Hey everyone, I'm back with a new version of this model!  The good news is that all of your suggestions really sped things up, it took ~2 days to finish, down from ~4 days from the original.  I probably don't need as many iterations, so it can go down even more in the future.

The current model is attached.  One improvement I'm trying to make (as suggested by Bob and others earlier today) is to pass all of the group variables in as a single matrix instead of the separate vectors, in order to improve readability of the model.  I started doing this but realized a problem: all of the alpha_* parameters are of variable length, due to the different number of levels in each of these groups.  Because of this, there can be no single matrix that can hold all the alphas.  Is that correct?  

If so, I wonder if it would be worth implementing a new data structure in future versions of Stan that would allow this functionality -- something like lists in R.  My C++ days are long behind me, but I remember linked lists and the like, maybe that could be done here ... spoken as someone who admittedly has no idea how complicated it would be.

Thanks,

-Yair

alpha_sex_eth ~ normal(0, sigma_sex_eth);

Also -- thanks for catching that bug!  I did add alpha_sex_eth[sex[i_n], eth[i_n]] twice.

Thanks again to everyone for your help!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Vectorizing over 2-dimensional structures in "deep interactions" model?
parts:
Sorry to lead you down a blind alley.

We indeed plan to implement ragged arrays. And
sparse vectors. And symmetric matrices and Cholesky factors.
So much to do...

It's not complicated because of the data structures
in C++ (std::vector is all you need), but more because
of the integration of all the types with Stan and Stan's I/O.
Also, there's the small issue of how to specify their sizes
or whether to allow unsized data structures through I/O.

There are various ways to code up ragged arrays currently,
but none of them let you do vector results easily.

- Bob
> On Tuesday, April 16, 2013 5:21:47 PM UTC-4, Yair wrote:

> The current model is attached. One improvement I'm trying to make (as suggested by Bob and others earlier today) is
> to pass all of the group variables in as a single matrix instead of the separate vectors, in order to improve
> readability of the model. I started doing this but realized a problem: all of the alpha_* parameters are of
> variable length, due to the different number of levels in each of these groups. Because of this, there can be no
> single matrix that can hold all the alphas. Is that correct?
>
> If so, I wonder if it would be worth implementing a new data structure in future versions of Stan that would allow
> this functionality -- something like lists in R. My C++ days are long behind me, but I remember linked lists and
> the like, maybe that could be done here ... spoken as someone who admittedly has no idea how complicated it would be.
